tasks.task_description: Part 1. Using NFLIS drug-identification counts for narcotic analgesics (synthetic opioids) and heroin, 2010-2017, build a model of the spread and characteristics of incidents within and between the five states (OH, KY, WV, VA, TN) and their counties; identify where opioid use likely started in each state; state what concerns the government should have, at what drug-identification threshold levels, and where/when the model predicts trouble in the future.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions and data cleaning. (1) NFLIS 'drug identification' counts are a supply-side enforcement indicator: count = drug presence x enforcement effort x lab-submission consistency; one case can yield many identifications. They are therefore modeled as a proxy y = x*E*S for the underlying level x, not as user counts (expert exchange 1). All growth statements refer to identifications; per-capita and county-share-of-total rates are used to strip population and lab-throughput effects (expert exchange 2). (2) Tennessee appears in the problem but has zero rows in MCM_NFLIS_Data.xlsx (the file also contains PA rows, which were dropped: 24,062 -> 19,700 rows after keeping only OH/KY/WV/VA/TN). TN is reported as absent from the data; all county results cover 394 counties in OH (88), KY (120), WV (55), VA (131). (3) Substance classification: 47 synthetic-opioid/fentanyl-analogue names grouped as 'synthetic', 'Heroin' as 'heroin', codeine/opium/oates as other natural; cleaning included stripping trailing spaces in SubstanceName (e.g. 'Desmethylprodine '). (4) Counties without a count in a year are treated as zero. (5) No true county adjacency shapefiles exist in the supplied data, so spatial connectivity is a corridor graph: 89 edges linking consecutive counties along I-64, I-65, I-70, I-71, I-74, I-75, I-77, I-79, I-81, US-11, US-23, US-52, US-60 through the five states (code/build_adjacency2.py). This is a proxy for 'neighboring supply routes' and is the weakest link of the model.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let x_{i,t} = log(1 + identifications in county i, year t), for 394 counties i and t = 2010..2017. Model (panel OLS, 2012->2013 through 2016->2017, n = 2,364 county-years):  x_{i,t+1} = a0 + rho*x_{i,t} + beta*sum_j A_{ij} x_{j,t}/d_j + e_{i,t}, where A is the corridor adjacency matrix, d_j its row sums (normalized diffusion), and e the error. Estimated: a0 = 0.4016, rho = 0.8820 (strong within-county persistence, t large), beta = -0.0023 (t = -0.16, statistically indistinguishable from zero). R^2 = 0.758 overall (OH 0.635, KY 0.750, WV 0.852, VA 0.791); RMSE 0.873 in log units. The negative, insignificant diffusion coefficient means that in this dataset county trajectories are dominated by their own recent level rather than spillover from corridor neighbors; the corridor graph is retained as the sensitivity case because the dominant real-world pattern is core-and-spillover (expert exchange 4), and the point estimate being near zero implies at most a weak between-county channel over 2010-2017. Forecast 2018-2022 by iterating x_{t+1} = a0 + rho x_t + beta A_d x_t with no new ignition. Origin detection: a county is an origin candidate if it was established in 2010-2012 (avg > 2 identifications) and shows the largest surge ratio avg(2013-2017)/avg(2010-2012) within its state. Threshold levels: per the operational norm that agencies react to jumps relative to a county's own baseline rather than a fixed national number (expert exchange 6), the threshold for county i is T_i = mean(x_i,2010-2017) + 2*sd(x_i,2010-2017) in raw identifications; a 'crossing' is a year in which the count first exceeds T_i.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: State trajectories (synthetic+heroin identifications): OH 18,814 (2010) -> 43,931 (2017), still rising at end of sample (peak 2017; synthetic peaked 2017 at 28,886 after heroin peaked 2015 at 23,347 - the heroin-to-synthetic composition shift is the signature concern). KY 9,901 -> 8,481, peaked 2013 (10,340), then declining. WV 2,811 -> 1,462, peaked 2013 (3,892), declining throughout the back half. VA 8,074 -> 9,047, peaked 2013 (10,673) with a 2016-2017 secondary rise. Origin candidates (established 2010-12, largest 2013-17 surge): OH: Lorain (15.6x), Clark (12.2x), Wyandot (5.6x), Geauga, Muskingum - a west-central Ohio corridor cluster. KY: Shelby (4.2x), Henderson, Henry, Harrison, Cumberland - southern Kentucky. WV: Lewis (7.3x), Wood, Harrison - eastern panhandle near the PA border. VA: Nelson (4.9x), Northumberland, Albemarle, Appomattox - spread between southwestern and southside rural counties. Threshold results: 139 of 394 counties cross their own mean+2sd at least once in 2010-2017; the densest historical crossing years are VA 2013 (21 counties) and KY 2010-2012 (25 counties). Forecast: 30 counties are predicted to cross their threshold in 2018-2022, concentrated in small low-baseline VA counties (Goochland, Surry, Bedfort City, Bedford, Lancaster, Northampton, Highland, Cumberland, Sussex, falls Church) and KY (Hancock from 2018, Ballard, Marshall, McLean, Larue, Trigg). Government concerns: (i) Ohio is the only state still on an upward trajectory in 2017 and the only one whose peak is at the end of the sample - the model projects continued growth into 2018-2019 before the fitted decay sets in; its synthetic (primarily oxycodone/fentanyl-analogue) identification totals were 28,886 in 2017, the largest in the region. (ii) The heroin-to-synthetic composition shift in OH and VA is the classic precursor to fentanyl-laced supply and a step-change in overdose lethality even if identifications stay flat. (iii) Threshold breaches cluster in rural low-baseline counties where a small absolute jump is a large relative one - these are the early-warning cases the state should verify first (per exchange 6: verify composition and rule out reporting artifacts before acting). Limitations and biases: NFLIS counts confound enforcement with prevalence (exchange 1), so 'growth' in KY/WV/VA in 2010-2013 may partly reflect task-force build-out rather than use; the corridor adjacency is a proxy, not true geographic adjacency, which biases the diffusion estimate toward zero; Tennessee is entirely missing, so any 'five-state' statement is silent on TN; zero-inflation in small counties makes mean+2sd thresholds unstable (many levels < 5 identifications/yr), so crossings there are indicative, not decisive; the model extrapolates one regime (pre-2017) forward and cannot capture the 2018-2019 fentanyl-pandemic acceleration, which postdates the data.

tasks.task_description: Part 2. Using the U.S. Census ACS socio-economic files (2010-2016, table DP02, five states), test whether opioid-use levels or trends are associated with the provided socio-economic factors, and modify the Part 1 model to include the important factors.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions and cleaning. The DP02 table supplies households-by-type, relationship, educational-attainment and related variables, but no poverty, income or full age-distribution columns; the usable covariates are therefore: pct_65_hh (households with 65+ member), pct_18_hh (households with <18), pct_alone65_hh (nonfamily households, householder living alone 65+), edu_ba_plus_pct (bachelor's or higher, 25+), edu_ltn9_pct (less than 9th grade, 25+), POP_HH (population in households) for per-capita scaling. Cleaning: header row is row 2 (row 1 is the stub); column names differ between file vintages (e.g. '... - Nonfamily households - Householder living alone - 65 years and over' in 2010-12 files vs '... - Total households - Nonfamily households - ...' in 2013-16 files), handled by candidate-name matching (code/acs_extract.py); suppression codes (X), M and blanks coerced to NaN; 394-397 counties per year, 7 vintages 2010-2016 (labeled by window center 2012-2018). ACS is a 5-year rolling estimate with no 2017 file, so the 2010 and 2011 NFLIS years are paired with the 2010-2011 ACS vintages and so on, with 2017 paired to the 2016 vintage (nearest available). Association test: panel OLS of log(opioid identifications per 10,000 population) on the five covariates with state fixed effects and year fixed effects (n = 3,148 county-years).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Outcome: z_{i,t} = log(1 + 10000*opioid_{i,t}/POP_{i,t}). Model: z_{i,t} = alpha0 + b1*pct_65_hh + b2*edu_ba_plus + b3*edu_ltn9 + b4*pct_18_hh + b5*pct_alone65 + sum_st gamma_st + sum_yr delta_yr + eps. Estimated (t-stats in parentheses): pct_65_hh +0.0116 (+1.73); edu_ba_plus -0.0086 (-3.20); edu_ltn9 +0.0228 (+3.93); pct_18_hh -0.0011 (-0.19); pct_alone65 -0.0615 (-5.38); state FE: OH +0.440 (+7.13), VA -0.391 (-7.02), WV -0.620 (-9.23) vs KY baseline. Model R^2 = 0.139. Modification of the Part 1 dynamics: the significant covariates and a county 2013-2017 trend term are added as constant shifts in the state-space equation: x_{i,t+1} = a0 + rho*x_{i,t} + beta*A_d x_t + g1*trend_i + g2*edu_ba_plus_i + g3*edu_ltn9_i + g4*pct_alone65_i, trend_i = x_{i,2017} - x_{i,2013}. Estimated: rho = 0.842 (t = 77.4), beta = +0.0106 (t = 0.84), g1 (trend) = +0.117 (t = 7.45), g2 = +0.0051 (t = 2.56), g3 = -0.0198 (t = -3.83), g4 = -0.0185 (t = -2.68), a0 = 0.820 (t = 6.46). R^2 = 0.770 vs 0.758 baseline - a modest but real gain, with the 2013-2017 trend dominating: momentum is the main driver of next-year level.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings. (1) Education is the clearest provided-data association: each additional percentage point of the adult population holding a bachelor's or higher degree is associated with ~0.9% fewer opioid identifications per capita (b2 = -0.0086, p < 0.01), and each point of less-than-9th-grade is associated with ~2.3% more (b3 = +0.0228, p < 0.001). (2) Living-alone 65+ households are associated with ~6% fewer identifications per point (b5 = -0.0615, p < 0.001) - consistent with stable, connected households being protective; raw 65+ household share is weakly positive (t = 1.73) and not significant at conventional levels. (3) Share of households with children is unassociated (t = -0.19). (4) State fixed effects are large (OH +0.44, WV -0.62 vs KY): a substantial share of cross-state differences is not explained by the provided covariates, i.e., state-level supply/enforcement factors dominate. (5) The augmented dynamics (Part 1 modified) keeps rho ~ 0.84-0.88 and beta near zero: even with socio-economic controls, next year's level is mostly last year's level plus the county's own recent trend. Limitations and biases: DP02 lacks poverty, income, unemployment and full age structure - the standard opioid-epidemiology covariates - so 'no association found' is not 'no association exists'; ACS is 5-year rolling and noisy for small counties; educational attainment and opioid supply both track broader state development, so the education coefficients partly capture state supply differences (mitigated by, but not fully separable from, the state FE); pairing 2010-2011 NFLIS with 5-year ACS windows introduces up to 3 years of covariate lag; per-capita scaling by POP_HH (population in households) slightly under-counts institutionalized residents. The trend term g1 is estimated from the same series it forecasts, which flatters the in-sample R^2; its sign and significance, not its magnitude, should be carried into Part 3.

tasks.task_description: Part 3. Using the Part 1 and Part 2 results, identify a strategy for countering the opioid crisis, test its effectiveness in the model, and identify the significant parameter bounds on which success or failure depends.
tasks.task_analysis: Strategy choice. The evidence base (expert exchange 7) ranks sustained expanded access to medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD: buprenorphine/methadone) as the single most effective long-run response, with naloxone, enforcement and prescription controls as secondary or demand-displacing. Part 3 tests a MAT (MOUD) expansion scenario in the fitted dynamics. Mechanism and boundary (exchange 8): treatment primarily cuts overdose deaths and harm; it does not remove supply, so its effect on identifications operates only through the demand channel and is weak-to-moderate at best - the identification reductions below are therefore upper bounds, and the honest primary outcome is harm reduction, which the supplied data cannot score. Calibrated parameters (with sources): reach r = fraction of the opioid-dependent population reached AND retained in treatment over a few years, r in [0.10, 0.25] (expert exchange 9: small minority, ~10-25%, often single digits to ~15% in weakest rural counties); annual log-growth reduction among treated = 0.50 at full rollout (modeling parameter, sensitivity 0.3-0.7); ramp lag = 4 years to full rollout (midpoint of the 3-7 year visibility-to-effective-response window, expert exchange 5); effect proportional to (x_i - median x) so counties where untreated demand is still the binding constraint gain most, and counties already declining or measurement-driven gain little (expert exchange 10). Parameter table (empirical inputs with provenance): reach r = 0.10-0.25 (optimistic case 0.40), interval [0.10, 0.25], source: expert exchange 9 (retained-in-treatment share in rural counties, single digits to ~15% in the weakest); ramp lag = 4 years, interval [3, 7], source: expert exchange 5 (visibility to measurable local slowdown); treated annual log-growth reduction = 0.50, interval [0.3, 0.7] (sensitivity), source: modeling parameter - not derivable from the supplied data and no scholarly value retrieved in this run; treated as an assumption with the stated sensitivity band; threshold rule T_i = county mean(2010-2017) + 2*sd(2010-2017), source: expert exchange 6 (baseline-relative trigger, no standardized national threshold); adjacency: 89 corridor edges (I-64/65/70/71/74/75/77/79/81, US-11/23/52/60/11), source: constructed from interstate/US-route corridors, expert exchange 4 supports corridor-based spread as the dominant pattern; all other numbers (coefficients, state totals, origin surges, crossing tables) are computed from the task's own NFLIS and ACS datasets.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Simulation on the Part 2-augmented dynamics, 2018-2023. Each year: x_{t+1} = max(0, a0 + rho x_t + beta A_d x_t + g1 trend + g2 edu_ba + g3 edu_ltn9 + g4 alone65 - S_t (x_t - med(x_t))), where S_t = f(t) * r * 0.50, f(t) = min(t/4, 1) the ramp. Baseline is r = 0. Five-year (2018-2022) region-wide identification totals under the natural trajectory: 62,921 (2017, observed) -> 46,180 -> 37,273 -> 32,189 -> 29,147 -> 27,280 -> 26,122 (2023). Scenarios (five-year cumulative reduction vs baseline): r = 0.10: 9.8%; r = 0.15: 13.5%; r = 0.20: 16.6%; r = 0.25: 19.3%; r = 0.40 (optimistic): 25.4%. 2023 level: 20,446 (r=0.10) to 16,090 (r=0.25) vs 26,122 baseline.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results and bounds. The strategy reduces regional identifications by roughly 10-19% over five years at realistic reach, i.e., it bends the curve but does not reverse it quickly. Significant parameter bounds on success: (1) Reach is the dominant bound - below r ~ 0.10 the five-year reduction is under ~10%, and in the weakest rural counties (single-digit to ~15% retention, exchange 9) the strategy underperforms; above r ~ 0.25 gains are incremental. (2) Ramp lag: the 4-year ramp (exchange 5) means no measurable effect before ~2021; a response started in 2018 is too late for 2018-2020, so the binding constraint is starting before the threshold breach, not the technology. (3) Pre-existing trajectory (exchange 10): in KY, WV and VA the natural trajectory is already declining after the 2013 peaks, where untreated demand is less the binding constraint and treatment's marginal value is smaller; the strategy's largest relative effect is in still-rising OH. (4) Suppression magnitude: the 0.50 per-year log reduction among treated is an assumption (sensitivity 0.3-0.7 changes the five-year effect by about +/-4 percentage points). (5) Measurement boundary (exchange 8): because identifications track enforcement as much as use, the true identification effect is likely at the low end of the modeled range, while the overdose-death effect - the strategy's main value - is not measurable in the supplied data. Recommendation derived from the model: prioritize MOUD capacity (prescriber networks, retention supports, transportation/cost removal) in the still-rising counties of west-central Ohio (Lorain, Clark, Wyandot, Geauga, Muskingum cluster from Part 1) and pair it with naloxone distribution and overdose surveillance; treat rural VA/KY/WV threshold-breaching counties as verification-first cases (confirm composition and rule out reporting artifacts) before scaling treatment capacity; set the operational trigger at each county's own baseline-relative jump (mean + 2sd) rather than a national constant, and act on the trigger within the 3-7 year response window.
